twitter.e: From Middle English twitren, twiteren, from Old English *twiterian, from Proto-West Germanic *twitwiʀōn, from Proto-Germanic *twitwizōną (“to chirp; twitter”). Cognate with Low German twitteren (“to twitter”), German zwitzern, zwitschern (“to twitter”). …

d.g: One who, or that which, twitters.
Alternative letter-case form of Twitterer.

twitterer.e: English twitter Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English twitterer From twitter + -er.

d.g: Something sold at a discount of two for the price of one.
Something that yields a substantial additional benefit; something that figuratively kills two birds with one stone.
d.x: Justice Clarence Thomas served up a twofer last week […]

d.g: The fashion of wearing long sleeves outside a short-sleeved shirt.
A cabling device used in theatre, allowing two stage lighting instruments to be connected to one dimmer.

twofer.e: Shortened form of two-for-one [deal], that is, two for the price of one (BOGO).

d.g: A British or Irish coin worth two (old or new) pence.
A cost or value of two pence.
A small amount or value.
Being or constituting a pair; two.
Twofold; double.
Performed by two individuals.
d.x: a twosome dance

d.g: A group of two; a pair; a couple; a group of two distinct individuals or components.

twosome.e: From Middle English twosome, equivalent to two + -some. Cognate with Scots twasome, twaesome (“twosome”).

d.g: To twiddle.
d.x: As it was, he tweedled the letter about in his hands for about five minutes, in a musing mood, and then stepped with it into Mr. Gammon's room.

d.g: To sell fake jewellery as genuine.
d.x: I am afraid that the knowing author of the “cracking a-crib” book would be flummoxed by tweedling.

d.g: To make a shrill or trilling sound
d.x: Yesterday I dined at the Percivals, and tweedled away upon a lovely harpsichord, and I was not bid to “mind my time.”

d.g: To say in a high-pitched voice.
d.x: "Oh, bien sur. Monsieur Raphael has only the kindest things to say," Azter tweedled. “Always.”

tweedle.e: said to be imitative, probably influenced by wheedle. Compare teedle, toodle, twiddle

d.g: To pluck or grasp using tweezers.
d.x: Stamp-men tweeze their treasures to avoid smudging, wear, tear; to hold them up to the light or pick them out of benzine baths in search of watermarks.

d.g: To shape by plucking out hairs with tweezers.
d.x: Here Mrs. Lawrence had smiled to soften the anxiety of her blue eyes under their frowning, carefully tweezed brows.

d.g: To pluck out hairs using tweezers.
d.x: Word to the wise: if you must tweeze solo, stick to plucking only the obvious stray hairs.
